instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

listeningScripts.title: Restaurant Reservation Issue
listeningScripts.text: Diner: Hi, I made a reservation for tonight at 7 PM under the name Anderson, and I just realized the name is spelled wrong in your system. Manager: Oh no, I'm sorry about that. Let me look that up. How is it spelled? Diner: A-N-D-E-R-S-O-N. I don't know how it got misspelled. Manager: I see it here as A-N-D-E-R-S-E-N. That's an easy mix-up. When you arrive, just let the host know and we'll get you seated right away. Diner: Actually, I'm calling because I need to change the time. Can I do 7:30 instead? Manager: Absolutely. Let me adjust that for you. How many people? Diner: Six of us. Manager: Perfect. I've moved you from 7 PM to 7:30 PM for six people, and I've corrected the name spelling. Is there anything else? Diner: Yes, one more thing. Can you make sure we have a quiet table? There are some business matters we want to discuss. Manager: I'll add a note to your reservation requesting a quieter area away from the bar. We have some nice tables by the window. Diner: That sounds great. What's your cancellation policy? Manager: We require 24 hours notice for cancellations. If you need to cancel, just call us before 7:30 PM tomorrow. Diner: Got it. Thank you.

listeningScripts.title: Music Concert Plans
listeningScripts.text: Alex: Are you going to the concert next Saturday? Casey: Which one? There are a few shows next weekend. Alex: The indie rock festival at the waterfront. Casey: Oh yeah, I've been thinking about it. How much are tickets? Alex: They're forty dollars each. Casey: That's not too bad. Who's performing? Alex: Five bands. The headliner is The Northern Stars. Casey: Oh, I love them. What time does it start? Alex: Six PM. It should wrap up around eleven. Casey: That's pretty late. Is there parking nearby? Alex: Yeah, there's a parking lot right by the venue. It's five dollars for the whole night. Casey: That's reasonable. Should we get food there or bring our own? Alex: They have food vendors there, but it's probably expensive. Casey: Let's grab something before we go then. Alex: Good idea. Want me to buy your ticket? Casey: Yeah, that would be great. Just send me the bill.

listeningScripts.title: University Orientation: First Week Checklist
listeningScripts.text: Hello, welcome to orientation week. I'm here to walk you through essential tasks for your first week. First, attend your faculty's orientation meeting on Monday at ten AM in the Student Centre. Bring your student ID. Second, register for your courses online by Wednesday, August 28th. Early registration means better class times. Third, purchase your textbooks from the university bookstore before classes start. Fourth, get your student photo ID taken at the Services Office between 9 and 4 on any day this week. The photo ID is required for library access and residence entry. Fifth, activate your email account at the IT support desk. Your email is your primary communication channel for all university announcements. Sixth, find your classes on a campus map. Most buildings are located around the central quad. Seventh, attend the Welcome Social on Friday evening in the gymnasium. It's a great way to meet other students and faculty. Eighth, complete your health and immunization form at Student Health Services. This is mandatory before attending classes. Finally, budget about three hundred dollars for books and materials. Questions? Visit the information desk in the main foyer.

listeningScripts.title: Nova Scotia Healthcare Worker Recruitment
listeningScripts.text: Nova Scotia is launching an aggressive recruitment campaign to address critical shortages in healthcare professionals. The province has announced a 35 million dollar investment in recruitment and retention initiatives. Currently, there are over 800 unfilled nursing positions across Nova Scotia hospitals and clinics. The campaign targets nurses, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, and laboratory technicians. Starting salaries for nurses are being increased by 12 percent to compete with other provinces. The government is also offering signing bonuses of up to 15,000 dollars for candidates relocating to rural communities. Housing assistance programs will help new recruits find affordable accommodation. International recruitment is underway, with partnerships established with nursing programs in the Philippines and India. Officials estimate it will take approximately 18 months to fill 60 percent of the vacant positions. Patient wait times have increased significantly due to staffing shortages, with some emergency departments reporting delays of four to six hours.

listeningScripts.title: University Program Expansion Planning
listeningScripts.text:
Dean Robert: We've been asked to consider expanding our engineering program, particularly in renewable energy studies. The faculty has requested three additional full-time instructors and funding for new laboratory equipment. The cost would be approximately 2.4 million dollars over two years. Given our current budget constraints, I'm hesitant to commit to this expansion.

Professor Elena: I understand the budget concerns, Dean, but we're actually losing enrollment to competing universities who offer these programs. Last year, we lost 150 potential engineering students to schools with stronger renewable energy options. If we don't expand now, we'll fall behind. Plus, there's significant industry demand for graduates with renewable energy expertise. Companies are specifically recruiting from universities with these specialized programs.

Student Representative Malik: From a student perspective, I absolutely support this expansion. Many of my classmates are interested in sustainability and green technology, but we don't have the courses or facilities to support that focus. I think this investment would make our university much more attractive to prospective students, which would actually increase our overall enrollment and revenue.

Budget Committee Member Diana: Malik makes a good point about revenue. If this program attracts even 200 additional students, the tuition revenue would exceed the expansion costs within three years. And we could explore partnerships with industry for funding. I've been in conversations with several renewable energy companies that might contribute equipment or funding in exchange for access to our graduates for recruitment.

listeningScripts.title: Digital Privacy in the Workplace
listeningScripts.text: I want to talk about something that concerns me deeply—workplace monitoring and digital privacy. Many companies today monitor their employees constantly: they track keystrokes, monitor websites visited, log bathroom breaks through card access, and even use AI to analyze email and chat conversations. The argument is usually that this improves productivity and security, but I think it's gone too far. Yes, employers have legitimate security concerns, but the level of surveillance we're accepting is unprecedented. When employees feel constantly watched, it creates anxiety and erodes trust. Studies show that excessive monitoring actually decreases productivity and morale. Workers spend time trying to appear productive rather than actually being productive. Moreover, there's a moral issue here. As an employee, you're a person, not a machine to be optimized. You deserve privacy and dignity at work. I'm not arguing against all monitoring—reasonable security measures are necessary. But there's a middle ground between trusting employees completely and treating them like suspects. Companies that have implemented less invasive monitoring policies actually report higher employee satisfaction and retention. So my position is this: employers should use targeted monitoring only where necessary for genuine security reasons, not blanket surveillance of everything everyone does. Trust and respect for employee privacy create better workplaces.
